newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - G7 to focus on currency rates, growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - G7 to focus on currency rates, growth.

text.p: Senior officials of the Group of Seven rich nations on Monday put worries about currency rates and economic growth squarely on the agenda for a meeting of the world's top finance officials in Berlin this weekend.

Details of the meeting of deputy finance ministers, which was held inside the Bundesbank in Germany's financial capital of Frankfurt, were not released and officials had no comment on the discussions.

But a German government source said the talks had focused on the state of the world economy and exchange rate developments, as well as international development aid and the need for closer cooperation between supervisory authorities.

German finance minister Theo Waigel said in an interview with Sunday's Berliner Morgenpost that these issues, together with Europe's plans to create a single currency, would be the focus of Sunday's meeting.
"The issues in our Berlin meeting will be the global economic conditions for growth, world trade, and of course exchange rates," Waigel told the newspaper.

He added, "Our colleagues from North America and Japan are very interested in receiving reports on the developments in Europe at first hand," he said. "That is why I have put the euro on the agenda for the meeting."
For financial markets, however, the immediate focus of the meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors is likely to lie in any comments on the U.S. dollar.

Markets are looking keenly for any hints that the Group of Seven -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- are dissatisfied with a roaring 6.5 percent rise in the dollar against the mark last month.

Although the G7 itself talked the U.S. currency higher after it plunged to all-time lows in 1995, some fear that the recent surge may have come a little too fast to appease the leading nations' concerns that markets are becoming disorderly.

Financier George Soros, who has made billions of dollars speculating in currency markets, said at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, on Monday that he believed the pace of change might be a source of concern for the G7 ministers.

European sources have indicated that they can live with the current dollar rate of around 1.65 marks, with France, concerned by the impact of a high franc rate on its exports, showing some tolerance on the upside of this.
Waigel, who said in Davos that he could live with current dollar rates, also noted in the newspaper interview that the dollar's rise was "good for German exports".
But Germany has also made clear that it will not be tolerate a bout of weakness in its currency.
Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, and other German central bank officials, sent a clear signal to markets last week that the dollar's rise could not go on at this space.
U.S. industry is also starting to feel the bite of the currency increase on its export trade.

Japanese prime minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Monday hinted at a compromise solution which would allow the G7 to brake the dollar's surge without sending it into a new downward spiral -- by endorsing the stability of the U.S. currency.
